text: Briarcliff Systems is moving a small application into Azure: a web tier customers reach directly, and an app tier that never should be reachable from the internet at all. This lab builds the whole environment from Chapters 1 through 6 — a tagged resource group, a two-subnet network, two VMs, and a storage account, all from the Azure CLI, in the order a real deployment follows.

Everything starts with one resource group, tagged the moment it's created — environment and costcenter tags that Lesson 31's cost investigation will search on later in this chapter. Then a single VNet, 10.20.0.0 slash 16, split into two slash-24 subnets: web-subnet for anything internet-facing, app-subnet for anything that shouldn't be. No security rules yet, just the shape of the network.

The web VM lands in web-subnet with a real public IP, because customers need to reach it directly. Standard_B2s, a burstable and inexpensive size, is plenty for a small front end — and cheap enough that it won't be the VM Lesson 31 has to chase down when the bill spikes.

The app VM goes in app-subnet with --public-ip-address left empty, on purpose. It only ever needs to hear from the web tier, never the internet, so it simply has no internet-facing address for anyone to attack. A Standard_LRS storage account holds the application's uploaded files and logs, kept off either VM's local disk entirely.

Five pieces, built in exactly this order: a tagged resource group, a VNet shaped into two subnets, a web VM with a public IP, an app VM with none, and a storage account for application data. Nothing here is secured yet, and nothing is being watched — that's deliberate, and it's exactly where the next lesson starts.

That's the environment standing. Next: locking it down with NSG rules that make the web and app boundary explicit, RBAC assignments scoped to the ops team, and the monitoring and budget alerts that catch problems automatically instead of by luck.
